hooks.text: A dead star is building a new planet from its own ashes.
Can a dying star forge a second generation of planets?
This star's death didn't destroy its planets; it created one.

title: The Star That Built a Second World
description: Astronomers discovered a second-generation planet forming from the chemical ruins of a dead white dwarf.

beats.text: A dead star is building a new planet from its own ashes.
beats.visual: artist concept of a white dwarf with a close-in gas giant exoplanet

beats.text: In 1999, the Hubble Space Telescope recorded one hundred mystery spectral lines around a cooling white dwarf.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope in orbit above Earth during mission STS-125

beats.text: For twenty-five years, these chemical fingerprints remained a total mystery that scientists could not decipher.
beats.visual: ultraviolet spectrum plot showing complex absorption lines from a white dwarf

beats.text: Using modern databases, University of Warwick researchers recently identified the mystery element as niobium.
beats.visual: wide view of the University of Warwick campus and researchers

beats.text: Niobium is a heavy metal forged only during the violent death throes of a dying star.
beats.visual: pure metallic sample of niobium crystal showing iridescent reflections

beats.text: The metal is being stripped from a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting just 3.7 million miles from the star.
beats.visual: artist concept of a planet losing its atmosphere with a comet-like tail near a star

beats.text: This gas giant is a rare second-generation world, born from the ruins of a destroyed solar system.
beats.visual: Hubble image of the Ring Nebula showing layers of shed stellar gas

beats.text: It orbits through a comet-like trail of dust, reclaiming the ashes of its past life.
beats.visual: artist concept of a debris disk and exoplanet orbiting a white dwarf

better_than_last: I moved technical catalog names to the on-screen card to keep the narrative audio punchy and avoid the retention drop-off associated with dense jargon in ep188.
